title: Surveillance: Exhibition Invitation
description:
Exhibition invitation for Lewis Stein: Surveillance at Mariposa Gallery, New York (September 8 - October 17, 2026).

The exhibition centers on Stein's 1984-85 photographic series documenting surveillance cameras throughout New York City. Stein captured these mechanical devices with a balance of criticality and humor. The deliberately grainy, large-scale photographs render the cameras almost quirky rather than menacing. By enlarging and blurring surveillance equipment, Stein's work confronts systems that quietly condition daily life.

Lewis Stein (1945-2022) was a New York-based photographer and conceptual artist. The Surveillance series was originally shown at Postmasters Gallery in 1985. The work remains prescient regarding pervasive surveillance culture. The exhibition also includes a 1968 readymade sculpture (a billy club suspended from a nail) exploring Stein's investigations of control systems.
notes: Exhibition invitation card. Mariposa Gallery, New York. September 8 - October 17, 2026.

title: Spray Can Sticker
description:
A die-cut vinyl sticker reproducing Roy Lichtenstein's Spray Can (1963), produced by the Brooklyn studio Apply and sold by the Whitney Museum shop.

The sticker is screen-printed on premium vinyl and die-cut to the image: a hand pressing the nozzle of an aerosol can, drawn in Lichtenstein's flat outline and Benday-dot manner. It measures 2.3 by 2.75 inches and is one of four Lichtenstein images Apply produced under license from the Estate of Roy Lichtenstein, with Drowning Girl, In the Car and I Love Liberty. The Whitney stocked the set in 2026 ahead of its retrospective Roy Lichtenstein: Like New (October 11, 2026 to May 10, 2027).

Lichtenstein (1923-1997) arrived at his signature manner in 1961: subjects lifted from comic strips and advertisements, painted in flat colour with hand-drawn Benday dots. By 1964 he was among the most recognised and most contested of the Pop artists. The Whitney holds 460 of his works, including the Roy Lichtenstein Study Collection given by the artist's foundation.

title: Drowning Girl Sticker
description:
A die-cut sticker of Roy Lichtenstein's Drowning Girl (1963), the comic-book painting now in the Museum of Modern Art, produced by the Brooklyn studio Apply and sold by the Whitney Museum shop.

Screen-printed on metallic poly and die-cut to the image, the sticker measures 3.5 by 3.5 inches. It reproduces the painting's weeping figure and speech balloon ("I don't care! I'd rather sink than call Brad for help!"), which Lichtenstein cropped from a panel in the DC romance comic Secret Hearts. Apply made it under license from the Estate of Roy Lichtenstein as part of a set of four Lichtenstein stickers. The Whitney stocked the set in 2026 ahead of its retrospective Roy Lichtenstein: Like New (October 11, 2026 to May 10, 2027), in which the painting is shown.

description:

title: In the Car Sticker
description:
A die-cut sticker of Roy Lichtenstein's In the Car (1963), one of the romance-comic paintings of his first Pop years, produced by the Brooklyn studio Apply and sold by the Whitney Museum shop.

Screen-printed on metallic poly and die-cut to the image, the sticker measures 3 by 2.6 inches. It reproduces the painting's blonde woman in a leopard coat and dark-haired man at the wheel, with speed lines across the window, a composition Lichtenstein took from a romance-comic panel. Apply made it under license from the Estate of Roy Lichtenstein as one of four Lichtenstein stickers. title: Temple Postcard
description:
An oversized postcard from the Whitney Museum shop reproducing Roy Lichtenstein's Temple (1964), an offset lithograph in the museum's Roy Lichtenstein Study Collection.

The image shows a ruined classical colonnade in black outline over a field of blue Benday dots: three columns and a broken entablature against a pale sky. Lichtenstein's lithograph was issued in 1964 both as a numbered edition and as an unsigned mailer announcing his exhibition at Leo Castelli Gallery, New York (October 24 to November 19, 1964). The Whitney's impression (2019.95) came as a gift of the Roy Lichtenstein Foundation and was shown in Order and Ornament: Roy Lichtenstein's Entablatures (2019-2020). The postcard was issued in 2026, ahead of the museum's retrospective Roy Lichtenstein: Like New (October 11, 2026 to May 10, 2027).

Lichtenstein (1923-1997) turned in 1961 to subjects taken from comics and advertisements, painted in a manner that imitated commercial printing. Classical architecture entered his work in 1964 with the temple images and returned later in the Entablature series. The Whitney holds 460 of his works and counts him, with Andy Warhol and James Rosenquist, among the key figures of Pop art.

title: Self-Portraits on Heel Pocket Notebook
description:
A pocket notebook from the Morgan Library & Museum's 2026 exhibition Hujar:Contact. Its cover is a full contact sheet of self-portraits Peter Hujar shot in his Second Avenue loft in 1974.

The sheet is job 620 in Hujar's numbering: three strips of square-format film, twelve frames, one of them blank. In ten he is shirtless in jeans against a white studio wall. He repeats one pose with small changes: a hand raised to his brow in a salute, a leg kicked back behind him. In the eleventh he stands square to the camera in the open loft, hands on his hips. Red editing marks flag a single frame in the middle strip. The back cover prints the museum's credit in white on black: Self-portraits on heel, 189 Second Avenue, 1974, Peter Hujar Collection, purchased on the Charina Endowment Fund, 2013 (2013.108:8.2109). Inside are 48 unlined pages.

Hujar (1934-1987) filed and numbered his contact sheets from the age of 21, and the Morgan holds more than 5,700 of them along with his job books. Hujar:Contact (May 22 to October 25, 2026), curated by Joel Smith, shows over 110 sheets beside 20 enlargements. Its catalogue, co-published with MACK, is also in the library. The shop listed the notebook on the day the exhibition opened.
tags: Photography, Peter Hujar, Contact Sheets, Self-Portraits, Notebooks, Ephemera, Museum Shop
notes: The library holds 30 copies. Morgan Shop SKU X14492, listed under the shop's Hujar:Contact collection. Back cover credit, as printed: "Peter Hujar (1934-187) / Self-portraits on heel, 189 Second Avenue, 1974, job 620 / Peter Hujar Collection, purchased on the Charina Endowoment Fund, 2013 / Morgan Library & Museum, 2013.108:8.2109 / Courtesy of Fraenkel Gallery, San Francisco and Ortuzar, New York; (c) The Peter Hujar Archive / Artists Rights Society (ARS)". The misprints "1934-187" and "Endowoment" are on the object. The shop does not state dimensions. Related catalogue record: Hujar:Contact (id 1797).

title: You Can't Drag Your Money Into The Grave With You [Postcard]
description:
A Fotofolio postcard of Barbara Kruger's Untitled (You can't drag your money into the grave with you), a 1988 paste-up that sets a slogan about money and death over a photograph of new leather shoes on grass.

The card reproduces the image in color at 11 by 15 cm. Three white bands cross the black-and-white photograph. Each carries part of the sentence in Kruger's white-on-red Futura Bold Oblique, so the phrase assembles itself as the eye moves down the picture. The source work is photograph and type on paper, 18 by 23 cm, now in the Pinault Collection. A 1990 screen print on vinyl enlarged the image to nearly three by four metres. Fotofolio, a New York postcard publisher founded in 1975, issues several of Kruger's images as cards.

Kruger, born in Newark in 1945, worked as a magazine designer before turning in the late 1970s to found photographs captioned with declarative text. This card sits with late-1980s works on money such as To Buy or Not to Buy and Bleed Us Dry.
tags: Art, Postcards, Ephemera, Barbara Kruger, Conceptual Art, Text Art, Feminism, Pictures Generation, Fotofolio, Printed Matter
notes: Acquired from Printed Matter, New York: https://www.printedmatter.org/catalog/58684. Not signed. Printed Matter stock 120603 C. Fotofolio postcard, color, 11 x 15 cm, reproducing Kruger's Untitled (You can't drag your money into the grave with you), 1988, photograph and type on paper, 18 x 23 cm, Pinault Collection; a 1990 screen print on vinyl of the same image exists. title: Untitled (Your assignment is to divide and conquer) [Postcard]
description:
A Fotofolio postcard reproducing Barbara Kruger's Untitled (Your assignment is to divide and conquer) (1981), one of the earliest of the red-bordered photograph-and-text works that have defined her practice since the early 1980s.

The image is a found black-and-white photograph of a man's face seen through the slats of a drawn blind. White Futura Bold Oblique runs across the top on a red band and the last word, "conquer," sits alone in a box at the foot of the picture. The source work, a photograph in the artist's frame at 147.3 by 103.8 cm, was shown at the Whitney's Downtown Branch in 1982 and illustrated in the catalogue of her 1983 ICA London show We Won't Play Nature to Your Culture.

Kruger (b. 1945) was a designer and picture editor at Condé Nast magazines before turning, around 1979, to found photographs overlaid with her own text. Fotofolio, founded in New York in 1975 by Julie Galant and Martin Bondell, issued several of her images as postcards alongside its history-of-photography series.

title: Men Don't Protect You Anymore Wooden Postcard
description:
A wooden postcard from Printed Matter carrying one sentence from Jenny Holzer's Survival series (1983-85), printed in red capitals across the grain of a thin sheet of wood.

The text reads MEN DON'T PROTECT YOU ANYMORE. Holzer wrote the Survival texts for electronic signs, after her first Spectacolor board in Times Square in 1982, and the sentences soon moved onto aluminium plaques, T-shirts and caps, and later onto stone benches. A 1984 plaque of this line stood on the sculpture plinth of Berlin's Museumsinsel from 2020. Printed Matter publishes the postcard with the artist at 10 x 15 cm, digitally printed, in a line of wooden postcards drawn from the Truisms and Survival series.

Holzer (b. 1950) began with the Truisms of 1977-79, anonymous broadsheets wheat-pasted around Manhattan, then the Inflammatory Essays (1979-82) and the Living plaques (1981). She won the Golden Lion at the 1990 Venice Biennale and has projected text onto buildings since 2001. The library also holds her Ivorypress box Belligerent (2017).
